blocks.text: Attitudes are 'learned predispositions to respond in a consistently favourable or unfavourable way towards a given object, person or event' (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975). An attitude is a combination of beliefs and values.

Beliefs are based on our knowledge of the world and link an object to an attribute; they are non-evaluative and objective (e.g. '**USA** is a nation built on capitalism'). Values relate to the importance or desirability of the object; they are largely subjective with preferential patterns attached (e.g. 'I do not like capitalism'). Values can turn beliefs into attitudes ('I dislike American people').

blocks.title: Three-component model of attitudes
rows: What the person feels about the object (favourable/unfavourable evaluations)
Thoughts, beliefs, knowledge about the object
Actual or intended responses to the object

blocks.title: Functions of attitudes (Katz)
rows: Attitudes are frames of reference that simplify the world and help make quick appraisals of situations
Reflect fundamental self-concepts; self-expressive and maintains personal integrity (e.g. vegetarianism)
Helps to function in a group setting; social acceptance
Protects from character or personal deficiencies; makes attitudes very resistant to change

blocks.mnemonic: KVSE: Knowledge, Value-expressive, Social adjustment, Ego-defensive
expansion: Ego-defensive: protects from deficiencies, resists change

bullets.text: Attitude = learned predisposition to respond favourably/unfavourably to an object, person or event (Fishbein & Ajzen 1975); a combination of beliefs and values.
Beliefs are objective and non-evaluative; values are subjective and evaluative, and turn beliefs into attitudes.
Three components: affective (feel), cognitive (think/know), behavioural (do).
Katz functions: knowledge, value expressive, social adjustment, ego-defensive (the last makes attitudes very resistant to change).

sections.title: 2. Why attitudes change: cognitive dissonance and self-perception

blocks.text: Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger): people strive for consistency between thoughts, feelings and actions. A discrepancy between attitudes (cognitive dissonance) or between attitudes and behaviours (attitude-behaviour discrepancy) initiates and drives either a change in attitudes (more common) or a change in behaviours.

Smoker example: the discrepancy between the cognition 'smoking is injurious' and the behaviour (repeated smoking) may lead to cutting down, or may alter the cognition ('there is too little evidence available to link smoking to poor health').

blocks.title: 1-Dollar / 20-Dollar experiment
rows: Paid $20 to say the task was fun and interesting
Did not develop dissonance (good incentive); lied but did not change belief that the task was boring; made situational attribution ('I did it for money, it was boring')
Paid $1 to say the task was fun and interesting

Experienced dissonance ('This task is boring' vs 'I am doing this without much incentive'); changed attitude and started liking the task; made dispositional attribution ('not much incentive, but I really liked it')

blocks.text: The experiment highlights the processes relating to counter-attitudinal behaviours.

blocks.title: Ways to reduce dissonance
rows: Primary attitudes get stronger afterwards (e.g. after betting on a horse, the belief that it will win strengthens)
Removal or denial of the dissonant cognition

blocks.text: Self-perception theory (Bem): self-report of attitude after a behaviour is usually an inference from one's own behaviour and context, which dissonance cannot explain adequately. Cognitive dissonance explains both counter-attitudinal behaviour and attitude-attitude discrepancy; self-perception applies better when attitude-congruent behaviour occurs, but it cannot explain attitude-attitude discrepancy.

blocks.title: Cognitive dissonance vs self-perception theory
rows: Both counter-attitudinal behaviour and attitude-attitude discrepancy
Drive for consistency changes attitude or behaviour
Attitude report is an inference from own behaviour and context

sections.title: 3. Measuring attitudes and the attitude-behaviour link

blocks.text: Attitudes are largely subjective and cannot be measured directly. Measures usually rely on self-report, assume the same statement has the same meaning for all respondents, and assume subjective attitudes can be quantified meaningfully. Observing behaviour is an alternative, but behaviours do not always reflect attitude.

blocks.title: Attitude scales
rows: Hundreds of statements scored by judges on an 11-point scale; about 10 statements from each extreme chosen for consistency of scores; each carries a value (average of 100 judgments); 20 statements make the scale; rarely used as too tedious; assumes the 11 points are intervals but they are really ordinal
Graded 'agree' to 'disagree'; one of the most popular and statistically more reliable measures; easy to construct; no assumptions about equality of intervals
Measures interpersonal attitudes in a repertory-grid-like way (who likes whom tables), called sociograms
Cumulative statements: accepting a statement usually means accepting all that come below it, step-wise

Measures verbally expressed attitudes; bipolar adjectives (e.g. evaluative good-bad, activity active-inactive, potency powerful-weak) on a 7-point scale; assumes every concept can be represented in a hypothetical semantic space with two extremes

blocks.title: Actual behaviour depends on (attitudes are only predispositions)

blocks.text: Attitudes and behaviours are not correlated in a simple linear fashion. If attitudes are measured with specified assessment of target, action, context and time element, measured attitudes will be closer to actual behaviour (e.g. attitude to legal abortion in a married woman after 3 months of marriage rather than abortion in general).

Single instances of behaviour are unreliable indicators of attitudes. Various attitudes aggregate to result in behaviour, and the strength of an attitude is proportional to its influence on behaviour.

**Q5**: an attitude scale with graded categories from strongly disagree to strongly agree is a Likert scale (not Thurstone); **Q46**: the semantic differential scale (7-point, bipolar adjectives) may be subject to positional response bias.

blocks.text: Gallup's 'touching the dot' experiments demonstrate self-recognition: a red dot is unknowingly placed on the child's face and a mirror shown. Only higher primates and humans older than 20 months successfully touch the dot; it does not occur below 15 months. 5 to ==25%== of infants touch the dot by 18 months and nearly ==75%== by 20 months, so self-recognition rapidly develops between 18 and 20 months. Object permanence is necessary for self-recognition.

Mirror recognition by primates may reflect behavioural recognition ('the one in the mirror is same as me') rather than self-recognition ('the one in the mirror is me'). Autobiographical memory in humans develops around age 3.5 to 4.5 years.

blocks.text: Attribution is the process of making judgments about causes of behaviour. Heider (1958) proposed the first psychological theory of attribution ('naive' or 'commonsense' psychology): people act like amateur scientists piecing together information until they reach a reasonable explanation. We distinguish intentional vs unintentional behaviours and make internal vs external attribution of cause.

Kelley's co-variation model: we tend to attribute behaviours to events that co-vary with those behaviours over time (if A occurs when behaviour B is observed, we assume A causes B). Three elements ensure validity of the inference.

blocks.title: Kelley's co-variation elements (student X late for a physiology lecture)
rows: Does everyone come late or only student X?
Does student X come late to other classes too?
Does student X come late to physiology lecture every time?

blocks.text: Consistency is most used in attribution; consensus is least used.

blocks.title: What each pattern leads to

Weiner: locus, stability, controllability; external stable uncontrollable cause for a negative event gives failure with anger.

blocks.title: Attribution biases
rows: Overestimating dispositional factors and not situational factors when attributing causes for others' behaviour; gives a sense of predictability about the other person; more pronounced if the behaviour is negative and undesirable
The person involved as agent attributes external causality; observers may invoke internal causality (intentional and dispositional)

The actor-observer effect is most pronounced for negative behaviours; may be absent or reversed for positive ones; offers self-enhancement and defence. Exception in depression: excessive self-blame for personal failures
'I am a just person living in a just world; everyone gets what they deserve'; 'bad things happen to bad people', leading to blaming-the-victim culture
False consensus effect / illusion of in-group homogeneity
Viewing another person's behaviour as representative of a group's behaviour (culture or racial stereotypes form)

rows: First impressions count more unless told to attend or observe repeatedly; a positive first impression is more likely to change than a negative one; primacy matters more with strangers, recency more with friends and repeated contacts

Perceiving others as wholly good or bad from a few observed traits (e.g. physical attractiveness); traits 'spill over' to the total perception. Investigators of crime suspects are susceptible, more accurately the reversed halo / devil effect / association fallacy

blocks.text: Theory of Mind (ToM) develops around age 3.5 to 4 years. It is the understanding that other persons have mental processes similar to one's own, and forms an essential part of the social attribution process.

Lack of development of ToM (trait related) could explain the apparent lack of empathy seen in autism. In acute psychosis, state-related ToM deficits are noted only when relapsing into positive symptoms (not pervasive). Poor ToM with reduced empathic ability is also demonstrated in conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder.

blocks.text: One-sided arguments may strengthen existing beliefs but two-sided arguments are more effective in changing beliefs/attitudes. Highly fear-inducing messages may increase anxiety without behaviour change (Jansis & Feshback 1953); moderately fear-inducing messages can produce greater behaviour change, giving an inverted U-shaped curve between fear and attitude/behaviour change. Feeling vulnerable also increases behaviour change.
The credibility of a perceived message is a key factor in persuasion (Hovland & Weiss 1951): a health report in a professional medical journal persuades more easily than one in a tabloid.
Propaganda is mass suggestion or influence via emotional manipulation. Education gives independence for making a judgment, whereas propaganda provides ready-made judgments to be adopted.

blocks.text: Conformity: no explicit requirement is made, but peer influence and the need for acceptance push one to carry out the task. Obedience: the individual is explicitly asked, and the instruction comes from an authority.

blocks.title: Conformity vs obedience
rows: A subject can influence others mutually

blocks.text: Conformity can be true internalisation of values or external compliance without changing private beliefs. Men conform less than women; people with lower intelligence, poorer ego strength, poor leadership abilities and inferiority feelings conform more often.

Sherif used the autokinetic effect (apparent false movement of a pinpoint of light in a dark room, aka Phi Phenomenon) to study conformity: individuals first gave idiosyncratic responses (individual norms), but when grouped together they modified their answers to conform and group norms emerged.

Asch used an unambiguous paradigm (length assessment test): group majority size up to 3 to 5 people influenced conformity, a much larger majority did not; the more unanimous the majority, the more the conformity; giving opinions privately reduced conformity; collectivist cultures showed more conformity than nuclear cultures.

Minorities can influence the majority if the minority is consistent, perceived to be autonomous with real interest in the issue, appears to have balanced flexibility, and appears to have some similarity to the rest of the group.

Milgram's obedience experiments: subjects, recruited by an authoritative university faculty, administered electric shocks by pressing buttons to victims in another room; the sham victim made crying sounds as the dose increased.

Acceptance of norms set by an influential person/group; content of the influence is intrinsically rewarding

Autocratic works if no input is needed; democratic is well regarded but time-consuming.

blocks.text: Prejudice is essentially an attitude. It can be positive or neutral as well as negative, though the term is mostly used for negative prejudice.

blocks.title: Components of prejudice
rows: According to Allport: anti-locution, avoidance, discrimination, physical attack, extermination (in increasing severity)

blocks.forTopic: Allport's five behaviours of prejudice (increasing severity)
blocks.mnemonic: AADPE: Always Avoid Dangerous People Everywhere

blocks.title: Theories of prejudice
rows: Authoritarians are prejudiced in a generalised manner; difficult upbringing and disciplinarian rules may lead to projection of difficulties onto minorities; does not explain sudden surges of prejudice in history; no experimental proof. An allied theory: ideological dogmatism in rigid, authoritarian people

When the source of extreme frustration is too powerful, aggression is displaced onto a soft target, the scapegoat; choice depends on the prevailing social mood, so society provides the content of prejudice while personality may predispose (Adorno)

Supplements scapegoating; discrepancy between actual attainments and expectations; acute changes cause sudden relative deprivation, unrest and scapegoating; subjective to individuals; may be within individuals (egoistic) or between groups (fraternalistic)
The mere suggestion of competition triggers prejudice; mere perception of another group's existence can spark discrimination
Positive self-image depends on personal and social identities, so individuals strive to improve their group's success, leading to prejudice against other groups

blocks.text: Robber's Cove summer camp: two groups made from unrelated individuals developed strong in-group preferences and anti out-group ideas even when allowed to interact freely; introducing competition produced a high degree of aggression and hatred. Sherif concluded mere competition is sufficient to create conflict and no real lack of resources or acute deprivation is needed.

blocks.title: Reducing prejudice
rows: Prejudice is lesser when a person has experienced it first hand: blue-eyed children were treated as inferior by brown-eyed pupils, and when roles were reversed the aggression shown was less
Contact between opposing groups under equal status in pursuit of common goals can reduce prejudice; personal friendship is not needed

blocks.text: Lack of knowledge about the other group produces a degree of autistic hostility, which reinforces negative stereotypes as a mirror-image phenomenon ('we are right, so they are wrong'); one group also comes to believe the opposite group's members are all alike (illusion of out-group homogeneity).
**Q27**: the behavioural component of Allport's prejudice is discrimination (stereotype is cognitive, hostility is affective).

bullets.text: Prejudice is an attitude: cognitive (stereotypes), affective (hostility), behavioural (Allport's five steps up to extermination).
Authoritarian personality (Adorno): generalised prejudice, no experimental proof; scapegoating: aggression displaced onto a soft target.
Relative deprivation: gap between attainments and expectations; egoistic (within individuals) or fraternalistic (between groups).
Realistic conflict (Robber's Cove): mere competition creates conflict; social identity theory: group success supports self-image.
Reduce prejudice by first-hand experience of prejudice (blue/brown eyes) and contact under equal status with common goals (Allport).
Mirror-image phenomenon and illusion of out-group homogeneity maintain autistic hostility.

blocks.title: Types of aggression
rows: Aimed solely at hurting someone; motivated by the need to express negative feelings such as anger
A means to an end (self-defence or to attain something), e.g. kidnapping for ransom; often planned, not impulsive
Violence for the sake of being violent; may be associated with pathological personality
Readily observable; reactive and impulsive or proactive and planned
Much more subtle (telling lies, spreading rumours, excluding a child from friends); seen more in girls than boys

blocks.title: Hydraulic (build-up) models
rows: Aggression is due to the death instinct Thanatos, an instinctive destructive urge that builds up and must be released
Natural selection: aggression ensures survival of the aggressor's genes (survival of the fittest)

Territorial imperative linked to survival benefits; aggression is a fixed action pattern elicited by sign stimuli; non-human aggression mostly constructive; ritualisation = stereotyped fights without actual harm; appeasement gestures (lying down, tucking the tail) reduce aggression

blocks.text: Non-hydraulic models refute the notion of 'building up' and 'release'.

blocks.title: Non-hydraulic models
rows: Controversial whether aggression is inherited; in humans people may inherit temperaments such as impulsiveness that make aggression more likely (Baron and Richardson 1994)

Children reproduce an aggressive model's acts, especially if the model's aggression was rewarded; vicarious conditioning = learning from seeing/hearing of others' consequences; performance is more likely if vicarious reinforcement was observed

Frustration always results in aggression and aggression occurs only with frustration; not true as frustration can produce depression or withdrawal; modified version: aggression is one of many possible products of frustration; Marcus-Newhall et al. (2000, 49 studies): displacement of aggression onto a less powerful or more accessible target
Frustration produces a readiness to respond aggressively; environmental cues (knives, guns) then lead to aggression; neither frustration nor cues alone suffice
Arousal from one source may energise another response: transferred excitation

In groups, sense of identity and belonging and diffusion of responsibility make people uncharacteristically aggressive; uniforms reduce individuality (police, military); does not always cause aggression

items.text: **Q16**: instrumental aggression is often planned (goal-directed, e.g. kidnapping for ransom); hostile/affective aggression is motivated by negative feelings.

bullets.text: Types: hostile (affective) vs instrumental (planned, goal-directed), positive, pathological, overt, covert (more in girls).
Hydraulic models: Thanatos, evolutionary theory, Lorenz (fixed action pattern, ritualisation, appeasement).
Non-hydraulic: genetic (inherit temperament such as impulsiveness), social learning (Bandura's Bobo doll, vicarious conditioning).
Frustration-aggression (Dollard) is modified: aggression is one of many products; displacement onto a less powerful target.
Berkowitz: weapons effect (frustration plus cues); Zillman: transferred excitation; Festinger: deindividuation.

sections.title: 16. Media, family and culture in aggression

blocks.text: Media influences on aggressive behaviour: **TV** can influence through modelling effects. In a natural experiment at St Helena Island when **TV** was first introduced, some increase in prosocial behaviour was surprisingly recorded.

blocks.title: Media influence is mediated via
rows: 'This is happening everywhere; it is not uncommon'
e.g. copycat crimes and suicides; Shannon Matthews incident in **UK** (2008) speculated to resemble a Channel 4 drama episode (Shameless)
Enhancing automatic associations of certain stimuli with a crime

blocks.text: Family background: aggressive children tend to commit violent and non-violent offences in adulthood; antisocial behaviour is much more common in men; harsh and inconsistent discipline and an absence of positive parenting may be aetiological factors.
Cultural differences: aggression is said to be much more common in individualist than in collectivist cultures (Oatley, 1993).

bullets.text: TV influences aggression through modelling; St Helena natural experiment surprisingly showed some increase in prosocial behaviour.
Media effects are mediated by arousal, disinhibition, imitation (copycat crime/suicide), desensitisation and priming.
Aggressive children commit violent and non-violent offences in adulthood; harsh, inconsistent discipline and lack of positive parenting are risk factors.
Aggression is said to be more common in individualist than collectivist cultures.

blocks.text: Dominance ranks influence the extent of sustaining stressors, but it is too simplistic to say that higher- or lower-ranking individuals have the highest stress or aggression; the actual level depends on the group's social structure and dynamics.

Ability to avoid confronting dominant individuals reduces stress; when this is lost in captivity, subordinates show high stress hormones (dominant wolves have more cortisol in the wild; subordinates have higher levels in captivity).

The most frequent context for aggression is defence of status, but the best fighter does not always become the highest-ranking individual (coalition formation and social support matter). In some species aggression is a primary cause of mortality.
The most important modulating influence on aggression is social dominance: once established, the rate of aggression drops substantially.

Aggressive encounters are highest among adolescent males during group migrations; aggression is also higher under crowding. Males are generally more aggressive than females, but once dominance is stabilised males show a substantial drop, leaving females as aggressive as or more than males.
Mating competition can increase male-to-male aggression; the presence of children can act as agonistic buffers reducing aggression in both sexes in some species.

Socially living primates learn social cues of aggression and restraint early by observing parents and older individuals, then practise with peers. Parental control is essential for the development of cortical areas involved in impulse control.

Coping outlets for stress include social support (grooming, coalition formation, physical contact); reconciliatory behaviour immediately after competition may help the loser cope. Poor availability of this support, with few kin, increases stress among subordinates.

**Q41** (primate psychology): the keyed answer is that aggression is higher during periods of instability such as rank transition (high cortisol and stress). The distractor 'young baboons learn appropriate expression of aggression by observing their peers' is not the answer; the notes (page 21) say primates learn by observing parents and older individuals, then practise with peers.

bullets.text: Stress and aggression depend on the group's social structure; neither high nor low rank is simply the most stressed.
Captivity removes the ability to avoid dominants: subordinates show high stress hormones (wolves: subordinates have more cortisol in captivity).
Social dominance is the most important modulator; once established, aggression drops substantially.
Aggression is highest in adolescent males during migrations and under crowding; presence of children can buffer aggression.
Young primates learn restraint from parents and older individuals; parental control is needed for cortical impulse-control development.
Social support (grooming, coalitions, contact) and reconciliation help subordinates cope.

sections.title: 18. Altruism, bystander behaviour and social loafing

blocks.text: Any action intended to help others is prosocial behaviour; altruism, the wish to help others with no expectation of reward, is often considered the motivation behind it.

blocks.title: Bystander phenomena
rows: When alone, individuals typically intervene when someone needs help
Intervention becomes less likely in a group, to the point that no single person from a crowd intervenes
Crowd members look at each other for signs of distress but remain calm themselves, wrongly appraising the situation as safe, so there is no intervention
Similar to social loafing: 'I have some responsibility, but so do others; let someone else help'
Not knowing what others are doing, one rationalises that someone would have helped the victim

blocks.text: Bystander competence is usually not required for intervention, except in ambiguous situations needing technical help (e.g. blood at the scene).

Arousal/cost-reward model: emotional arousal on seeing a victim increases motivation to act, but a cognitive appraisal of costs and rewards precedes intervention. If the cost of helping is high, the bystander reinterprets the situation: calling it non-urgent, blaming the victim, or diffusing or dissolving responsibility.
Males show higher agentic help and intervention, while females show higher communal help and empathy.
Social loafing (Ringelmann's effect) is seen in tug-of-war and clapping after a performance: the larger the group, the less the individual performance, as one thinks the others will do the job.

bullets.text: Altruism = wish to help with no expectation of reward; prosocial behaviour = any action intended to help.
Bystander apathy (Genovese effect): the more observers, the less likely anyone intervenes; pluralistic ignorance = misreading calm others as meaning safe.
Diffusion of responsibility ('someone else will help') vs dissolution (assuming someone already helped).
Arousal/cost-reward model: high cost leads to reinterpretation (non-urgent, blame the victim, diffuse responsibility).
Males give more agentic help; females more communal help and empathy.
Social loafing (Ringelmann): individual effort falls as group size rises.
